paras.text: Welcome to policy interpretation. This is the chapter that decides every other chapter. Before you can argue a deadline, a bad faith claim, or an appraisal fight, you have to know how a Michigan court actually reads the words in the contract. Let's build it case by case, in the order Michigan courts apply them.

Start with the single most important rule in Michigan insurance law: Rory versus Continental Insurance Company, Michigan Supreme Court, July twenty eighth, two thousand five. The dispute was a one year deadline to sue under an auto policy, but the holding reaches every policy. Unambiguous contracts, including insurance policies, are enforced as written unless a provision violates a law or public policy. Then the court went further: judicial determinations of reasonableness are an invalid basis to refuse to enforce an unambiguous contract provision. A judge cannot look at a clear policy term, decide it seems unfair, and rewrite it. Rory shut a door lower courts had been using to strike inconvenient policy language as unreasonable. If you remember one sentence from this chapter, remember this: unambiguous language wins, and fairness is not a legal argument.

Now a doctrine Michigan explicitly rejects, because other states use it and it will trip you up if you assume it applies here. Some states let an insured argue that even though the policy says one thing, a reasonable policyholder expected something broader, and courts should honor that expectation instead of the words on the page. That is the reasonable expectations doctrine. Michigan does not have it. Wilkie versus Auto Owners Insurance Company, Michigan Supreme Court, July sixteenth, two thousand three, held flatly that the rule of reasonable expectations has no application in Michigan, and overruled the prior cases that had recognized it. So if a homeowner says, I always assumed my policy covered this, that is not a legal theory in Michigan. Sympathetic, maybe, but it does not move an unambiguous exclusion.

So if reasonable expectations does not work, what does an insured do when policy language genuinely conflicts with itself? That is Klapp versus United Insurance Group Agency, Michigan Supreme Court, June eighteenth, two thousand three. Memorize the citation, because this one gets mangled constantly. Four hundred sixty eight Michigan four hundred fifty nine. Not four sixteen. Four fifty nine. Klapp defines ambiguity this way: a contract is ambiguous when its provisions are capable of conflicting interpretations. If two clauses in the same policy irreconcilably conflict, the policy is ambiguous. Here is the part everybody gets wrong. Finding an ambiguity does not mean the insured wins. Klapp sets an order of operations. First the factfinder looks at extrinsic evidence, meaning things outside the four corners of the policy: the application, correspondence with the agent, industry custom, anything showing what the parties actually intended. If that evidence answers the question, that answer controls, even if it favors the insurance company. Only after all of that fails does contra proferentem apply, the rule that ambiguous language is construed against whoever drafted it, almost always the insurer. Klapp calls contra proferentem a tie breaker, used only after conventional interpretation, including extrinsic evidence, has been tried and found wanting.

Next, who has to prove what when a claim gets denied. This is Heniser versus Frankenmuth Mutual Insurance Company, Michigan Supreme Court, July sixth, nineteen ninety five. Heniser sets up a two step relay race. Step one: it is the insured's burden to establish that the claim falls within the terms of the policy. Step two, only after step one is satisfied: whether that coverage is negated by an exclusion. Now read Heniser carefully, because this is where a lot of study material goes wrong. Heniser gives you the order and the insured's half of the burden, and nothing more. It never says the insurer carries the burden on the exclusion. For that half you cite Hunt versus Drielick, four hundred ninety six Michigan three hundred sixty six, two thousand fourteen, which restates Heniser's test and then quotes an older case, Fresard, for the rule that the insurer should bear the burden of proving an absence of coverage. Hunt adds the counterweights: exclusionary clauses are strictly construed in favor of the insured, but clear and specific exclusions must be enforced. Heniser for step one, Hunt for step two. If the carrier cannot prove the exclusion fits the facts, the insured's initial showing of coverage stands and the claim is owed.

A related question comes up in almost every real dispute. Suppose the insurer proves an exclusion applies, but that exclusion has its own exception, something like an ensuing loss clause. Whose burden is the exception? Logically the insured's, since the insured benefits. But no controlling Michigan case squarely holding that was opened this session. Know the logic, do not quote a Michigan case name for it.

Moving on to waiver and estoppel, where insureds try to argue their way into coverage that was never sold to them. Kirschner versus Process Design Associates, Michigan Supreme Court, May eleventh, nineteen ninety nine, is the controlling case. The key word is usually, and notice it every time you see this case cited. Kirschner holds that the application of waiver and estoppel is limited, and usually the doctrines will not be applied to broaden coverage to protect the insured against risks that were not included in the policy or that were expressly excluded. Why not? Because, in the court's words, an insurance company should not be required to pay for a loss for which it has charged no premium. You cannot get coverage for free just because someone at the insurance company said something careless on the phone.

But usually is not never. Kirschner points to two situations where courts have let waiver or estoppel work: where the insurance company misrepresented the terms of the policy, and where the insurer defended the insured in a liability case without reserving the right to later deny coverage. Even then it takes a showing that the inequity to the insured outweighs the inequity to the insurer, and Kirschner applied neither exception on its own facts. Outside those patterns, a verbal assurance from an adjuster almost never survives, which is why you get coverage commitments in writing. If an adjuster says, do not worry, we will cover the detached garage, and there is no endorsement for it, that promise is not enough on its own.

Now overhead and profit, where restoration contractors and public adjusters spend a lot of energy. The case is Salesin versus State Farm Fire and Casualty Company, Michigan Court of Appeals, April twenty first, nineteen ninety eight, published. Salesin repaired his own home instead of hiring a general contractor, and State Farm argued that since he never actually paid a contractor's overhead and profit, he should not be paid for it. The court rejected that, holding that not actually incurring the cost is, in its words, not dispositive. It adopted a test from a Pennsylvania case, Gilderman: repair or replacement costs include any cost the insured is reasonably likely to incur, and in some instances that includes a general contractor and his twenty percent overhead and profit.

Here is the trap. Salesin does not create an automatic rule that overhead and profit is always owed. The court said so directly: Gilderman does not support the position that overhead and profit should always and automatically be included in an actual cash value payment. The test is whether a general contractor was reasonably likely to be needed for that scope, not whether one was hired. A single trade repair, say just replacing carpet, is a weak case. A multi trade rebuild, roofing, drywall, flooring, and paint in sequence, is exactly the situation Gilderman and Salesin describe, where a homeowner is reasonably likely to need someone coordinating trades, so overhead and profit belongs in the payment regardless of who swings the hammer. Match the argument to the scope of work, not to a blanket rule.

Now the doctrine that decides who wins when a covered peril and an excluded peril combine to produce one loss. Three competing legal tools fight over the outcome. Concurrent causation says a covered peril's contribution alone triggers coverage. Efficient proximate cause says the dominant cause that started the chain controls the whole loss. An anti concurrent causation clause, an A C C clause, is language the insurer writes into an exclusion to shut both doctrines off, by saying the exclusion applies regardless of any other cause, whether it acted before, during, or after the excluded peril.

Michigan's controlling authority is Sunshine Motors Incorporated versus New Hampshire Insurance Company, Michigan Court of Appeals, February twenty second, nineteen ninety five, published. A car dealership flooded when heavy rain combined with a piece of wood partially blocking the local drainage system. The insured argued the blocked drain was a separate, non excluded cause. The court disagreed, because the exclusion carried exactly the anti concurrent causation language just described: coverage excluded regardless of any other cause or event contributing concurrently or in any sequence to the loss. Whether the blocked drain was a direct or indirect cause, the principal factor or merely a contributing factor, made no difference. The policy expressly excluded coverage either way.

Be honest about the limits. Sunshine Motors is a Court of Appeals decision and it is carrier favorable. But the Supreme Court has spoken on the underlying doctrine and went the same direction. In Vanguard Insurance Company versus Clarke, four hundred thirty eight Michigan four hundred sixty three, nineteen ninety one, a Court of Appeals panel used what the Supreme Court called the minority rule of concurrent causation to defeat an auto related exclusion in a homeowner's liability policy. The Supreme Court reversed, saying it discerned no compelling legal or policy basis for that doctrine to nullify an unambiguous exclusion. Vanguard is a liability case, not a first party property case, so do not oversell it. But between the two, no Michigan case adopting a broad, pro coverage concurrent causation doctrine, the way Florida's Sebo decision did, was found this session. One argument does survive: you can try to segregate damage caused solely by the covered peril. That rests on the exclusion's own caused by wording, not on any Michigan case found this run, so do not claim a Michigan court has blessed it.

Now a phrase you will see in almost every business income and civil authority form: direct physical loss of or damage to property. Michigan's leading statement on it comes out of the COVID nineteen wave. Gavrilides Management Company versus Michigan Insurance Company, Michigan Court of Appeals docket number three five four four one eight, published February first, twenty twenty two. Two Lansing area restaurants were closed by the governor's pandemic orders and sought business income coverage, arguing the closure itself was a direct physical loss. The court disagreed. Here is its actual language, because a wrong paraphrase of this case circulates widely. The court said the word physical necessarily requires the loss or damage to have some manner of tangible and measurable presence or effect in, on, or to the premises. The restaurants, it said, were unambiguously closed by impersonal operation of a general law, not because anything about or inside the premises had physically changed. Now the part people get backwards. Gavrilides did not stop at the coverage trigger. The plaintiffs asked to amend to allege the virus was physically present, so the court said it was necessary to address that alternative basis for denying coverage, and in a separate section held that the defendant properly denied the claim pursuant to the virus exclusion. Two holdings, not one. The lesson generalizes well beyond COVID: direct physical loss requires something tangible and measurable in, on, or to the premises. A legal restriction on how the property may be used, without more, does not meet that bar in Michigan.

Let's close with actual cash value and the numbers to memorize. Michigan Compiled Laws section five hundred point twenty eight thirty three, subsection one, paragraph a, sets a statutory floor: every fire insurance policy in Michigan must provide, at a minimum, coverage for the actual cash value of the property at the time of the loss. Notice what it does not do. It sets a floor but never defines how actual cash value is calculated. That gap is what the Department of Insurance and Financial Services, D I F S, addressed in Bulletin twenty twenty four dash twenty six dash I N S, issued November eighth, twenty twenty four. The bulletin describes actual cash value as ordinarily meaning the loss of value due to wear and tear, deterioration, and obsolescence to physical or tangible items. Then it makes the key move: nontangible items, defined as labor, taxes, fees, and overhead and profit, are not physical objects, and do not deteriorate, age, or decline in value the way a roof or a carpet does.

Here is the trap. For personal lines homeowners or dwelling policies issued or renewed effective July first, twenty twenty five or after, an insurer that wants to depreciate a nontangible item in an actual cash value payment can only do so through a standalone endorsement identifying those items, not by burying it in the policy form's definitions. That endorsement has to be optional, and because it reduces coverage, it has to be offered with a commensurate premium reduction. What the bulletin does not do is ban depreciating labor, taxes, fees, or overhead and profit. It conditions the practice on transparency. And remember the instrument hierarchy: a bulletin is guidance from the D I F S director, not a statute. D I F S superseded an earlier bulletin, twenty twenty four dash eighteen dash I N S, through that same administrative process, no legislative vote required.

One more structural point, and this one is industry background, not Michigan law. A named peril policy lists the perils it covers, and anything left off the list is not covered. An open peril policy, sometimes called special form or all risk, covers everything except what is specifically excluded. You saw that grant quoted in Gavrilides: covered causes of loss means risks of direct physical loss, unless excluded or limited. The common H O three form splits the difference: dwelling and other structures are open peril, personal property is typically named peril unless the homeowner upgrades.

Let's recap. Rory, two thousand five: unambiguous contracts enforced as written, no judicial reasonableness override. Wilkie, two thousand three: no reasonable expectations doctrine in Michigan. Klapp, four sixty eight Michigan four fifty nine, two thousand three: contra proferentem is a last resort tie breaker, after extrinsic evidence. Heniser, nineteen ninety five: insured proves coverage first. Hunt versus Drielick, two thousand fourteen: insurer proves the absence of coverage. Kirschner, nineteen ninety nine: waiver and estoppel usually will not broaden coverage. Salesin, nineteen ninety eight: self performance is not dispositive on overhead and profit, but there is no automatic rule. Sunshine Motors, nineteen ninety five: anti concurrent causation clauses are enforced where they actually appear in the exclusion at issue. Vanguard, nineteen ninety one: the Supreme Court will not let concurrent causation nullify an unambiguous exclusion. Gavrilides, twenty twenty two: direct physical loss needs something tangible and measurable in, on, or to the premises, and that same opinion separately enforced the virus exclusion. Bulletin twenty twenty four dash twenty six dash I N S: a standalone, optional, premium reduced endorsement before an insurer depreciates labor, taxes, fees, or overhead and profit, on policies issued or renewed on or after July first, twenty twenty five. Learn this chapter cold, because every other chapter in this track assumes you already know how Michigan reads a policy.
